en: [1] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:

[2] "Monks, there are these five points that should be frequently reflected upon by a householder or one who has gone forth. What are the five? 'I am subject to illness; I have not transcended the nature of being subject to illness'—this point should be frequently reflected upon by a householder or one who has gone forth."

Subject to aging and subject to death, one will undergo separation, dissociation, parting, and disjunction from all that is desired, beloved, dear, and pleasing; one is the owner of one's own actions, born of action, the heir of action, and the refuge in action. Therefore, whether as a householder or as one who has gone forth, one should constantly reflect on this point: "Whatever action I shall perform—whether virtuous or evil—I shall become the recipient of the fruit of that very action."

[3] For what purpose, whether one is a householder or one who has gone forth, should this point be repeatedly reflected upon: "I am subject to illness; I have not transcended the nature of being subject to illness"?

Indeed, there exists among sentient beings a pride of health regarding their health, intoxicated by which they engage in misconduct with body, speech, and mind. Having engaged in misconduct with body, speech, and mind, on that account and by that condition, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in the hells.

For those who constantly reflect upon this point, that intoxication with health which exists in health will pass away. With this purpose in mind—that "I am subject to illness and have not transcended the nature of illness"—whether one is a householder or a renunciant, this point should be reflected upon constantly. [4] And with what purpose in mind should a householder or a renunciant constantly reflect upon this point, thinking: "I am subject to old age and have not transcended the nature of old age"?

Indeed, among sentient beings there exists in youth the intoxication of youth; intoxicated by that pride, sentient beings engage in misconduct with the body, and they engage in misconduct with speech and mind. Having engaged in misconduct with body, speech, and mind, on account of that cause and that condition, after the dissolution of the body, following death, they are reborn in states of deprivation, in miserable destinies, in the abyss, in the hells.

For those who constantly reflect upon this state, whatever pride of youth they may have in their youth will pass away. With this purpose in mind—that "I am subject to old age and have not transcended the nature of aging"—this state should be reflected upon constantly by one who is either a householder or a renunciant.

[5] For what purpose, and with what underlying reason, should a householder or one who has gone forth repeatedly reflect upon this point: "I am subject to death; I have not transcended the nature of mortality"? Indeed, there exists among sentient beings an intoxication with life, by which intoxication sentient beings, being intoxicated, engage in misconduct with the body, engage in misconduct with speech, and engage in misconduct with the mind.

Having practiced misconduct with the body, and having practiced misconduct with speech and mind, they—on account of that cause and on account of that condition—after the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in the hells. For those who constantly contemplate this situation, whatever pride of life there was regarding life will depart. It is for this purpose—that "I am subject to death and have not transcended the nature of mortality"—that this situation should be constantly contemplated by one who is either a householder or one who has gone forth.

[6] For what purpose should this state be constantly contemplated by one who is either a householder or a renunciant: that there will be separation, dissociation, parting, and disjunction from all things that are desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing?

Indeed, for all beings, there will be a state of becoming otherwise, a state of separation, a parting, and a dissociation from those things that are desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing to the mind. Whether one is a householder or a renunciant, this fact must be constantly contemplated. Indeed, regarding those things that are desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing to the mind, beings possess desire, passion, affection, love, attachment, fixation, or obsession.

For those who constantly reflect upon this state, whatever desire, passion, affection, love, attachment, fixation, or obsession they have toward things that are wished for, lovely, dear, and pleasing will be repelled.

With this purpose in mind—that there will be separation, dissociation, parting, and disjunction from all things wished for, lovely, dear, and pleasing—whether one is a householder or a renunciant, this state should be reflected upon constantly.

[7] And for what purpose should one—whether a householder or one who has gone forth—constantly reflect on this point: "I am the owner of my actions, I am born of my actions, I am the heir to my actions, and I have my actions as my refuge; whatever action I shall perform, whether virtuous or evil, I shall become the partaker of that very action."

"There is bodily misconduct and there is the ripening of bodily misconduct; there is verbal and mental misconduct and there is the ripening of verbal and mental misconduct; there is bodily good conduct and there is the ripening of bodily good conduct; there is verbal and mental good conduct and there is the ripening of verbal and mental good conduct. Having thus eliminated manifold sinful and unwholesome states, I shall proceed by undertaking manifold wholesome states.

In view of this significant purpose, whether one is a householder or a renunciant, one should constantly reflect on this point: "I am the owner of my actions, I am born of my actions, I am the heir to my actions, and I have my actions as my refuge; whatever action I shall perform, whether virtuous or evil, I shall become the partaker of that very action."

[8] In this regard, monks, the learned noble disciple trains himself thus: "It is not only I who am subject to illness and have not transcended the nature of illness; rather, as far as there is any coming, going, staying, passing away, or rebirth of sentient beings, all sentient beings are subject to illness and have not transcended the nature of illness. For one who knows thus and sees thus, the path arises for the abandonment of the fetters.

Namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. He cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that arisen path. As he cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that arisen path, his fetters are abandoned or become attenuated.

[9] In this regard, the learned noble disciple trains himself thus: "It is not I alone who am subject to old age and subject to death. It is not for me alone that there will be a state of becoming otherwise, a separation, a parting, and a dissociation from all that is cherished, beloved, dear, and pleasing."

Indeed, it is not I alone who am the owner of my actions, born of my actions, the heir of my actions, and the refuge in my actions; rather, as far as there is any coming or going, staying, passing away, or rebirth among sentient beings, all sentient beings are owners of their actions, born of their actions, heirs of their actions, and refuges in their actions. Whatever action they shall perform—whether wholesome or evil—they will become partakers of the fruit of that very action.

For one who knows thus and sees thus, the path arises for the abandonment of the fetters; namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. He cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that arisen path.
As he cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that arisen path, his fetters are abandoned or become attenuated.
[10] Thus spoke the Blessed One; with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
